amami-shima.name: Amami Ōshima
amami-shima.summary: The largest island in Japan's Amami archipelago, between Kyūshū and Okinawa, home to about 73,000 people, much of it within a national park.

wasanbon.name: Wasanbon
wasanbon.summary: A fine-grained Japanese sugar traditionally made in Shikoku since about the 1770s, prized for use in wagashi sweets.

wagashi.name: Wagashi
wagashi.summary: Traditional Japanese confectionery made mainly from plant-based ingredients using pre-Western cooking methods, often served with green tea; most modern forms developed in the Edo period (1603-1868).

japanese-curry.name: Karē
japanese-curry.summary: Japanese curry, adapted from Indian cuisine introduced by the British, usually served as curry rice, curry udon or curry-filled bread, and now one of Japan's most popular dishes.

hotteok.name: Hotteok
hotteok.summary: A filled pancake popular as street food in South Korea, originating in Qing dynasty China and brought to Joseon Korea in the 19th century.

japanese-chinese-cuisine.name: Japanese Chinese cuisine
japanese-chinese-cuisine.summary: Fusion of Japanese and Chinese culinary traditions developed since the late 19th century, mostly rooted in Cantonese cuisine and served in ramen shops, dim sum houses and Chinese-style restaurants.

cantonese-cuisine.name: Cantonese cuisine
cantonese-cuisine.summary: The cuisine of Cantonese-speaking people from China's Guangdong province, one of China's Eight Great Traditions and, through emigration, the style behind most Chinese restaurants in the West until the late 20th century.

imo-incident.name: Imo Incident
imo-incident.summary: A violent 1882 uprising by unpaid Joseon soldiers in Seoul, sparked partly by reforms and Japanese military influence, in which rioters killed officials and attacked the Japanese legation.

y-shoku.name: Yōshoku
y-shoku.summary: A style of Western-influenced Japanese cooking that emerged during the Meiji Restoration, adapting European dishes under Japanese names written in katakana.

meiji-era.name: Meiji era
meiji-era.summary: Period of Japanese history (1868–1912) under Emperor Meiji, when Japan moved from an isolated feudal society to a modern, industrialized world power.

josiah-conder-architect.name: Josiah Conder
josiah-conder-architect.summary: British-French architect (1852–1920) hired by Meiji Japan to teach architecture and design public buildings in Tokyo, earning him the nickname 'father of Japanese modern architecture.'

tatsuno-kingo.name: Tatsuno Kingo
tatsuno-kingo.summary: Japanese architect (1854–1919) who designed the Bank of Japan building and Tokyo Station's Marunouchi building, and served as dean of Tokyo Imperial University's Architecture Department.

tatsuz.name: Sone Tatsuzō
tatsuz.summary: Japanese architect who lived from 1853 to 1937.

katayama-t-kuma.name: Katayama Tōkuma
katayama-t-kuma.summary: A Japanese architect (1854–1917) who designed the Nara and Kyoto Imperial Museums and helped introduce French-influenced Western architecture to Japan after assisting Josiah Conder on major building projects.

centennial-exposition.name: Centennial International Exhibition
centennial-exposition.summary: The first official world's fair held in the United States, staged in Philadelphia in 1876 to mark the centennial of the Declaration of Independence, drawing nearly 10 million visitors from 37 countries.

imperial-household-artist.name: Teishitsu Gigeiin
imperial-household-artist.summary: Title officially given to artists appointed by Japan's Imperial Household Agency to create works for the imperial palace; 70 artists held it between 1890 and 1944.

shibata-zeshin.name: Shibata Zeshin
shibata-zeshin.summary: A Japanese lacquer painter and print artist (1807–1891) of the late Edo and early Meiji periods, often called Japan's greatest lacquerer.

namikawa-yasuyuki.name: Namikawa Yasuyuki
namikawa-yasuyuki.summary: Japanese cloisonné artist (1845–1927), one of the two most famous enamellers of the 1890s–1910s 'golden age,' appointed an Imperial Household Artist in 1896.

japanese-western-eclectic-architecture.name: Japanese-Western Eclectic Architecture
japanese-western-eclectic-architecture.summary: An architectural style deliberately combining Japanese and Western elements, emerging in Yokohama during the 1853–1867 Bakumatsu period and spreading after the 1868 Meiji Restoration.

bakumatsu.name: Bakumatsu
bakumatsu.summary: The final years of Japan's Edo period, 1853 to 1867, when foreign pressure ended Japan's isolation and the Tokugawa shogunate gave way to the modern Meiji empire.

meiji-restoration.name: Meiji Restoration
meiji-restoration.summary: The 1868 political restoration of imperial rule in Japan, ending shogunate control and starting the country's rapid modernization and Westernization.

japan-art-academy.name: Japan Art Academy
japan-art-academy.summary: Japan's highest-ranking official arts organization, known as the Imperial Fine Arts Academy from 1919 and the Imperial Art Academy from 1937 before taking its current name after World War II.

john-ruskin.name: John Ruskin
john-ruskin.summary: English polymath (1819–1900) — writer, art critic and philanthropist — hugely influential through the early 20th century, later seen as anticipating environmentalism.

nara-national-museum.name: Nara National Museum
nara-national-museum.summary: One of Japan's most prominent national art museums.

kyoto-national-museum.name: Kyoto National Museum
kyoto-national-museum.summary: One of Japan's major art museums, located in Kyoto and focused on pre-modern Japanese and Asian art.

mitsui.name: Mitsui Group
mitsui.summary: A group of autonomous Japanese multinational companies, including major trading, banking, paper and chemical firms.

kaichi-school.name: Kaichi School
kaichi-school.summary: One of Japan's first schools, opened in Matsumoto in 1873; its 1876 Western-style building is a National Treasure, now an education museum.

japan-art-association.name: Japan Art Association
japan-art-association.summary: Traditionalist Japanese art organization tracing back to 1879, which promoted exhibitions, later founded the Ueno Royal Museum, and today organizes the Praemium Imperiale award.

prince-arisugawa-taruhito.name: Prince Arisugawa Taruhito
prince-arisugawa-taruhito.summary: A Japanese imperial prince and army general, 1835 to 1895, who commanded during the Boshin War and Satsuma Rebellion and held senior government posts in the Meiji era.

manchuria.name: Manchuria
manchuria.summary: A historical region of Northeast Asia covering present-day Northeast China and parts of the Russian Far East, the homeland of the Manchu people who founded the Qing dynasty.

korean-empire.name: Korean Empire
korean-empire.summary: Korean monarchical state proclaimed in 1897 by King Gojong, marked by the modernizing Gwangmu Reform, ending with Japan's annexation of Korea in 1910.

liaodong-peninsula.name: Liaodong
liaodong-peninsula.summary: A peninsula and historic region in Northeast China east of the Liao River, whose name comes from an ancient commandery and which was long contested by Chinese and Korean powers.

shenyang.name: Shenyang (Mukden)
shenyang.summary: A major city in northeastern China, formerly known by its Manchu name Mukden, long fought over by Ming, Qing, Russian and Japanese forces.

weihai.name: Weihai
weihai.summary: Seaport city in Shandong province, China, formerly called Weihaiwei, and the closest mainland Chinese city to South Korea.

tokugawa-shogunate.name: Tokugawa shogunate
tokugawa-shogunate.summary: Japan's military government from 1603 to 1868, founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu; enforced isolationist policies and a strict class system until its overthrow in the 1868 Meiji Restoration.

jules-brunet.name: Jules Brunet
jules-brunet.summary: A French military officer (1838–1911) who trained the Tokugawa shogunate's army, then fought alongside the rebel Republic of Ezo in Japan's Boshin War before returning to serve in the Franco-Prussian War.

imperial-japanese-army.name: Imperial Japanese Army
imperial-japanese-army.summary: Main ground force of the Empire of Japan from 1871 to 1945, modernized after the Meiji Restoration and central to Japan's wars until its surrender in World War II.

pacific-fleet-russia.name: Pacific Fleet (Russia)
pacific-fleet-russia.summary: The Russian Navy's fleet in the Pacific Ocean, established in 1731 and headquartered in Vladivostok.

yalu-river.name: Yalu River
yalu-river.summary: River forming part of the border between China and North Korea, alongside the Tumen River and Paektu Mountain; its valley has seen several military conflicts.

incheon.name: Incheon
incheon.summary: City in northwestern South Korea near Seoul, which grew from a small port town in 1883 into the country's third-most-populous city and a major economic hub.

tonghak-peasant-revolution.name: Tonghak Peasant Revolution
tonghak-peasant-revolution.summary: A Korean peasant uprising of 1894–1895 led by followers of the Tonghak movement, whose suppression drew in Chinese and Japanese troops and helped trigger the First Sino-Japanese War.

satsuma-rebellion.name: Satsuma Rebellion
satsuma-rebellion.summary: An 1877 revolt of disaffected samurai against Japan's new Meiji government, crushed after nine months; it ended the samurai class and ushered in a conscript-based modern army.

saig-takamori.name: Saigō Takamori
saig-takamori.summary: A Japanese samurai and politician (1828-1877) who helped overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868, then led the failed Satsuma Rebellion against the new Meiji government in 1877, dying in the fighting.

imperial-japanese-army-academy.name: Imperial Japanese Army Academy
imperial-japanese-army-academy.summary: Principal officer training school for the Imperial Japanese Army, offering a junior course for cadets and a senior course for officer candidates.

hong-ky-ngnae.name: Hong Gyeong-rae
hong-ky-ngnae.summary: Rebel leader in Pyongan Province, Joseon Korea (1780 to 1812), who led a rebellion against oppressive taxation and government treatment before being killed in battle.

baltic-fleet.name: Baltic Fleet
baltic-fleet.summary: The Russian Navy's fleet in the Baltic Sea, founded in 1703 by Peter the Great as the oldest Russian fleet; it passed through the Soviet era and is now based in Kaliningrad.

combined-fleet.name: Combined Fleet
combined-fleet.summary: The main sea-going force of the Imperial Japanese Navy, made a permanent organization only from 1933 after earlier existing as a temporary wartime command.

battle-of-tsushima.name: Battle of Tsushima
battle-of-tsushima.summary: The final, decisive naval battle of the Russo-Japanese War in May 1905, in which Japan's fleet destroyed Russia's Baltic Fleet after its seven-month voyage, the first major clash of modern steel battleship fleets.

theodore-roosevelt.name: Theodore Roosevelt
theodore-roosevelt.summary: 26th president of the United States (1901–1909), who became president after William McKinley's assassination and, before politics, wrote a history of the Naval War of 1812.

treaty-of-portsmouth.name: Treaty of Portsmouth
treaty-of-portsmouth.summary: 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War, negotiated with US President Theodore Roosevelt's help; it gave Japan dominance in Korea, the Liaodong lease and southern Sakhalin.

battle-of-pungdo.name: Battle of Pungdo
battle-of-pungdo.summary: The first naval battle of the First Sino-Japanese War, fought 25 July 1894 off Korea's coast, in which Japanese cruisers engaged China's Beiyang Fleet as both powers vied for influence over Korea.

heungseon-daewongun.name: Heungseon Daewongun
heungseon-daewongun.summary: Title of Yi Ha-eung, regent of Joseon Korea during his son Gojong's minority in the 1860s and the dominant political figure of an era of Western pressure and internal poverty.

french-expedition-to-korea.name: French expedition to Korea
french-expedition-to-korea.summary: An 1866 French punitive expedition against Joseon Korea over the execution of French missionaries, ending in French retreat and confirming Korea's isolationism for another decade.

shogun.name: Shogun
shogun.summary: Title of Japan's military rulers from 1185 to 1868, who governed through the bakufu (their military government) while nominally appointed by the Emperor.

natsume-s-seki.name: Natsume Sōseki
natsume-s-seki.summary: Japanese novelist, poet and scholar (1867 to 1916), often called the first modern novelist of Japan, known for works including I Am a Cat, Botchan and Kokoro.

mori-gai.name: Mori Ōgai
mori-gai.summary: Japanese army surgeon general, translator, novelist and poet (1862–1922) who introduced German literature to Japan and helped modernize Japanese literature.

naoya-shiga.name: Naoya Shiga
naoya-shiga.summary: A Japanese writer (1883–1971) active in the Taishō and Shōwa periods, known for a lucid, straightforward style and strongly autobiographical fiction.

i-novel.name: I-novel
i-novel.summary: Japanese literary genre of confessional fiction closely based on the author's own life, which emerged from the Meiji-era reception of Western naturalism.

takizawa-bakin.name: Kyokutei Bakin
takizawa-bakin.summary: Japanese novelist of the Edo period (1767–1848), regarded as a leading author of his time, best known for the 106-book epic Nansō Satomi Hakkenden.

nans-satomi-hakkenden.name: Nansō Satomi Hakkenden
nans-satomi-hakkenden.summary: An epic Japanese novel by Kyokutei Bakin, published over 28 years from 1814 to 1842, considered the largest novel in Japanese literary history.

yomihon.name: Yomihon
yomihon.summary: Genre of Japanese book from the Edo period, emphasizing text over illustration and often featuring Buddhist ethics and supernatural or historical themes.

go-gawa-poetry-club.name: Go Gawa poetry club
go-gawa-poetry-club.summary: A poetry club in Edo, Japan, in the early 19th century, whose members wrote poems on illustrated prints and had met 1,600 times by 1836.

surimono.name: Surimono
surimono.summary: A genre of privately commissioned Japanese woodblock prints, often made for the New Year, notable for experimental subjects and lavish printing techniques; popular from the 1790s to the 1830s.

t-son-shimazaki.name: Tōson Shimazaki
t-son-shimazaki.summary: Pen name of Japanese writer Haruki Shimazaki (1872 to 1943), who began as a Romantic poet and became a leading figure of Japanese Naturalism, best known for the novel Before the Dawn.

bungakukai.name: Bungakukai
bungakukai.summary: Japanese monthly literary magazine, published by Bungeishunjū and focused on "pure literature."

the-dancing-girl-short-story.name: The Dancing Girl
the-dancing-girl-short-story.summary: Mori Ōgai's first published short story (1890), based on his own experiences as a medical student in Germany, foreshadowing Puccini's Madama Butterfly with reversed roles.

botchan.name: Botchan
botchan.summary: A 1906 novel by Japanese author Natsume Sōseki centered on morality, mixed with humor and sarcasm, and one of the most widely read Japanese novels.

kokoro.name: Kokoro
kokoro.summary: A 1914 novel by Natsume Sōseki about a young man's bond with an older "Sensei" hiding a secret about a friend's death; one of Japan's best-selling novels.

light-and-darkness-novel.name: Light and Darkness
light-and-darkness-novel.summary: A 1916 Japanese novel by Natsume Sōseki, his final work, left unfinished at the time of his death.

hy-banki.name: Hyōbanki
hy-banki.summary: Published rankings and critiques of kabuki actors and courtesans in Edo-period Japan, issued at New Year in Edo and Kamigata, a key part of urban popular culture alongside ukiyo-e prints.

turtle-ship.name: turtle ship
turtle-ship.summary: A type of Korean warship used by the Joseon Navy from the early 15th into the 19th century, named for its shell-like covering and sometimes, uncertainly, described as an early ironclad.

louis-mile-bertin.name: Bertin
louis-mile-bertin.summary: French naval engineer (1840–1924), one of the foremost of his time, who championed fast, powerfully armed light warships over large battleships.

imperial-japanese-navy.name: Imperial Japanese Navy
imperial-japanese-navy.summary: Navy of the Empire of Japan from 1871 to 1945, the world's third-largest navy by 1920 and the main opponent of Allied forces in the Pacific War.

jules-verne.name: Jules Verne
jules-verne.summary: French novelist, poet and playwright, 1828 to 1905, whose adventure novels such as Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas made him one of the most translated authors ever.

around-the-world-in-eighty-days.name: Around the World in Eighty Days
around-the-world-in-eighty-days.summary: Adventure novel by Jules Verne, published in 1872, about Phileas Fogg's wager to circle the globe in eighty days.
around-the-world-in-eighty-days.source_title: Around the World in Eighty Days

lyon.name: Lyon
lyon.summary: France's third-largest city, at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers; it was capital of the Gauls under Rome and later became a major economic hub during the Renaissance, noted for its cuisine.

yokohama.name: Yokohama
yokohama.summary: Japan's second-largest city, on Tokyo Bay near Tokyo, opened to Western trade in 1859 and since grown into a major cosmopolitan port.

general-sherman-incident.name: General Sherman Incident
general-sherman-incident.summary: The 1866 destruction of an American merchant ship on Korea's Taedong River after its crew ignored orders not to trade, an early clash in Korea's isolationist policy.

shunr-oshikawa.name: Shunrō Oshikawa
shunr-oshikawa.summary: Japanese author, journalist and editor (1876-1914), best known as a pioneer of Japanese science fiction.

japan-korea-treaty-of-1876.name: Japan–Korea Treaty of 1876
japan-korea-treaty-of-1876.summary: An 1876 treaty between the Empire of Japan and the Kingdom of Joseon forcing Korea open to Japanese trade, after Japan sent a warship to survey its coast without permission.

it-hirobumi.name: Itō Hirobumi
it-hirobumi.summary: A Japanese statesman who served as Japan's first prime minister from 1885 to 1888 and three more times between 1892 and 1901, and who played a central role in drafting the 1889 Meiji Constitution; he lived 1841–1909.

japanese-resident-general-of-korea.name: Resident-General of Korea
japanese-resident-general-of-korea.summary: Official post overseeing Japan's protectorate over Korea from 1905 to 1910.

an-jung-geun.name: An Jung-geun
an-jung-geun.summary: Korean independence activist who assassinated former Japanese Prime Minister Itō Hirobumi in Harbin in 1909 and was executed by Japanese imperial forces in 1910.

harbin.name: Harbin
harbin.summary: Capital of Heilongjiang province in northeastern China, founded in 1898 with the Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway and once home to a large Russian immigrant community.

matthew-c-perry.name: Matthew C. Perry
matthew-c-perry.summary: American naval officer (1794–1858) who led the expedition that ended Japan's isolation and signed the 1854 Convention of Kanagawa opening it to the U.S.

yi-wanyong.name: Yi Wanyong
yi-wanyong.summary: Korea's 7th Prime Minister (1858-1926), remembered for signing the treaties that placed Korea under Japanese rule in 1910; his name became a byword for Korean collaboration with Japan.

terauchi-masatake.name: Terauchi Masatake
terauchi-masatake.summary: A Japanese military officer and politician who served as prime minister of Japan from 1916 to 1918, and held the rank of Marshal in the Imperial Japanese Army.

governor-general-of-ch-sen.name: Governor-General of Chōsen
governor-general-of-ch-sen.summary: The chief administrator of Japan's colonial government in Korea from 1910 to 1945, appointed from Tokyo and responsible for infrastructure, justice, censorship and suppressing Korean independence efforts.

gojong-of-korea.name: Gojong
gojong-of-korea.summary: Penultimate Korean monarch (1852–1919), ruling 1864–1907 first as king of Joseon and then as the first emperor of the Korean Empire, amid growing Japanese pressure.

sakhalin.name: Sakhalin
sakhalin.summary: Large island in Northeast Asia, now part of Russia, whose ownership was contested among China, Russia, and Japan over the past millennium.

kuril-islands.name: Kuril Islands
kuril-islands.summary: A volcanic archipelago of 56 islands stretching between Japan's Hokkaido and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, under Russian administration since a 1945 Soviet invasion and still disputed by Japan.

treaty-of-saint-petersburg-1875.name: Treaty of Saint Petersburg (1875)
treaty-of-saint-petersburg-1875.summary: 1875 treaty in which Japan ceded the part of Sakhalin island it held to Russia in exchange for the Kuril Islands.

karafuto-prefecture.name: Karafuto Prefecture
karafuto-prefecture.summary: A Japanese colonial prefecture established in 1907 to govern southern Sakhalin after the Russo-Japanese War, occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1945.

japan-korea-treaty-of-1905.name: Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905
japan-korea-treaty-of-1905.summary: A 1905 treaty, also called the Eulsa Treaty, that stripped Korea of its diplomatic sovereignty and made it a Japanese protectorate, following Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War.

hully-ndae.name: Hullyŏndae
hully-ndae.summary: A Japanese-trained infantry regiment of the Joseon Army established in 1895, whose troops stormed the royal palace and enabled Japanese assassins to kill Queen Min before the regiment was dissolved later that year.

r-nin.name: Rōnin
r-nin.summary: A samurai left without a lord or master, typically after the lord's death or loss of favor, in Japan between 1185 and 1868.

empress-myeongseong.name: Empress Myeongseong
empress-myeongseong.summary: Wife of King Gojong of Joseon and queen from 1866 until her assassination in 1895, known during her lifetime as Queen Min; she favored gradual modernization against Japanese influence.

li-hongzhang.name: Li Hongzhang
li-hongzhang.summary: Chinese statesman of the late Qing dynasty (1823-1901), nicknamed the 'Oriental Bismarck,' who led the Self-Strengthening Movement and founded the Beiyang Fleet.

yuan-shikai.name: Yuan Shikai
yuan-shikai.summary: A Chinese general and statesman (1859–1916) who secured the Qing abdication, became the Republic of China's first formal president, and briefly declared himself emperor in 1915.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

kabo-reform.name: Gabo Reform
kabo-reform.summary: Series of sweeping reforms in Korea, 1894 to 1896, under King Gojong, launched in response to the Donghak Peasant Revolution.

ch-oe-cheu.name: Choe Je-u
ch-oe-cheu.summary: A Korean religious leader (1824-1864) who founded the Donghak movement, blending shamanism, Daoism, Buddhism and Confucianism, and was executed for allegedly preaching heretical teachings.

yangban.name: Yangban
yangban.summary: The hereditary scholar-official aristocracy that ruled Joseon-era Korea, serving as government administrators overseeing its agrarian bureaucracy into the 20th century.

tonghak.name: Tonghak
tonghak.summary: A Korean Neo-Confucian reform movement founded in 1860 as a reaction to Western influence, which later evolved into the religion known as Cheondoism.

seohak.name: Seohak
seohak.summary: The introduction of Western technology, philosophy and, most notably, Catholicism to Joseon Korea in the 18th century; its opposite was the traditional 'Eastern learning,' Donghak.

kyoto-school.name: Kyoto School
kyoto-school.summary: A Japanese philosophical movement centered at Kyoto University that blended Western philosophy with East Asian religious and moral thought, beginning around 1913 with founder Kitarō Nishida.

kitar-nishida.name: Kitarō Nishida
kitar-nishida.summary: A Japanese moral philosopher who lived from 1870 to 1945 and founded the Kyoto School of philosophy, teaching at Kyoto University after graduating from the University of Tokyo in 1894.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

tenrikyo.name: Tenrikyo
tenrikyo.summary: A Japanese new religion arising from the 19th-century teachings of Nakayama Miki, centered on cultivating a 'Joyous Life' through charity and mindfulness.

kurozumiky.name: Kurozumikyō
kurozumiky.summary: A Shinto-based Japanese new religion founded in Okayama in the 19th century after its founder, Munetada Kurozumi, claimed a divine union with the sun goddess Amaterasu in 1814.

oomoto.name: Oomoto
oomoto.summary: Shinto-based Japanese new religion founded in the 1890s by Deguchi Nao and Deguchi Onisaburō, notable for promoting Esperanto and interfaith dialogue.

k-toku-sh-sui.name: Kōtoku Shūsui
k-toku-sh-sui.summary: A Japanese socialist and anarchist (1871–1911) who helped introduce anarchism to Japan, opposed the Russo-Japanese War, and was executed for alleged involvement in a plot to assassinate the emperor.

high-treason-incident.name: High Treason Incident
high-treason-incident.summary: A 1910 socialist-anarchist plot to assassinate Japan's Emperor Meiji, leading to mass arrests of leftists and the execution of 12 alleged conspirators in 1911.

son-byong-hi.name: Son Byong-hi
son-byong-hi.summary: Korean religious leader and independence activist (1861–1922) who led the Donghak movement, later renamed it Cheondoism, and worked to distance it from Japanese influence.

cheondoism.name: Cheondoism
cheondoism.summary: A 20th-century Korean religion based on the 19th-century Donghak movement, renamed in 1905; it holds that humans and things are generated by a God-nature present in all beings rather than created by a supernatural god.

hajime-kawakami.name: Hajime Kawakami
hajime-kawakami.summary: A Japanese professor and economist (1879–1946) who studied Marxism and became active in Japanese communism, translating major economic works and writing on poverty and social reform.

abdurreshid-ibrahim.name: Abdurreshid Ibrahim
abdurreshid-ibrahim.summary: Tatar Muslim scholar, journalist and traveller (1857–1944) who worked to unite Crimean Tatars and became the first imam of the Tokyo Mosque after visiting Japan.

horace-wilson-professor.name: Horace Wilson
horace-wilson-professor.summary: American expatriate educator in late 19th-century Japan credited with introducing the sport of baseball there.

kaisei-academy.name: Kaisei Academy
kaisei-academy.summary: Private secondary school for boys in Tokyo, where American teacher Horace Wilson introduced baseball as a school sport in 1872.

treaty-ports.name: Treaty ports
treaty-ports.summary: Sea ports in China, Japan and Korea opened to foreign trade in the 1800s, mainly through unequal treaties forced on those countries by Western powers.

sencha.name: Sencha
sencha.summary: A Japanese green tea made by infusing whole processed leaves in hot water, unlike powdered matcha; it is the most popular tea in Japan.

shinbutsu-bunri.name: Kami and Buddhas Separation Act
shinbutsu-bunri.summary: A Meiji-era policy, formally known as shinbutsu bunri, that separated Shinto kami from Buddhas and Buddhist temples from Shinto shrines after over a thousand years of blending.

yokohama-country-athletic-club.name: Yokohama Country & Athletic Club
yokohama-country-athletic-club.summary: Sports club in Yokohama, Japan, founded in 1868 as the Yokohama Cricket Club by Scottish cricketer James Pender Mollison, later merging with other sports clubs.

gyokuro.name: Gyokuro
gyokuro.summary: A shade-grown Japanese green tea whose production dates to the 1830s, distinct from sun-grown sencha and prized for its distinctive flavour.

tsuneo-matsudaira.name: Tsuneo Matsudaira
tsuneo-matsudaira.summary: Japanese diplomat and politician (1877–1949) who served as ambassador to the United States and Britain before becoming the first President of Japan's House of Councillors.

korea_japan-industrial-science-006: Around the World in Eighty Days
